strengths: The paper identifies a relevant failure mode for computer vision: removing spurious correlations does not ensure robustness when learned invariant cues disappear through occlusion or cropping. The motivating example clearly explains the value of learning multiple predictive cues.

H-CMNIST provides a useful controlled diagnostic. In Table 1, ASGDRO improves shape-only accuracy over GDRO from 61.44±1.03% to 69.17±6.19%, while retaining nearly perfect performance when color is available. This supports improved learning of the harder feature.

The empirical evaluation is broad and supports practical usefulness. ASGDRO improves GDRO's worst-group accuracy from 87.2% to 91.0% on CelebA and from 90.6% to 91.4% on Waterbirds. Table 4 reports 65.9% average DomainBed accuracy and improves DPLCLIP from 72.6% to 74.0%. WILDS experiments provide further evidence across different shifts.

The optimizer is straightforward to integrate into existing training pipelines. The manuscript includes pseudocode, a code link, substantial hyperparameter and model-selection details, and results across three seeds. Hessian measurements provide supporting evidence that the resulting solutions have lower curvature across groups.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 does not hold as stated. In Appendix A.4, the classifier is theta=lambda with sum(lambda)=1 and risk R(theta)=0.5(Y-sum(theta))². Taking Y=1, every simplex lambda has zero risk, and its maximum risk under ||epsilon||₂≤rho equals rho²p/2, independently of lambda. Thus single-feature and uniformly balanced predictors are equally optimal. The proof introduces a lambda-dependent gradient factor without justification. An adaptive perturbation constraint would require a different analysis. This directly undermines the central feature-balancing guarantee.

The reduction from SIL to parameter-space sharpness has additional substantive gaps. Joint conditional invariance in Definition 1 does not imply that every feature subset is invariant or equally predictive, as asserted in Section 3.2. Appendix A.2 does not establish the claimed representation of subset mechanisms through parameter interpolation. Furthermore, low risk along interpolation paths does not establish low risk throughout the enclosing ball; the equality between the finite mechanism maximum and the ball maximum in Section 3.3 is generally only an inequality. Consequently, the proposed objective is not established as achieving Definition 3.

The implementation differs materially from the analyzed objective. Section 3.5 uses one perturbation computed from average empirical risk in every non-toy experiment, whereas the objective and Algorithm 1 use separate adversarial perturbations for each environment. Opposing group gradients can cancel in the average, leaving important adverse directions unexplored. No approximation bound or comparison with separate perturbations establishes that the practical version retains the claimed behavior across environments.

The experiments support improved robustness more convincingly than the claimed SIL mechanism. H-CMNIST is the only direct feature-removal evaluation; real-image results use standard shift benchmarks, Grad-CAM visualizations, and Hessian measurements. These do not establish that multiple independently predictive cues are learned or that predictions survive their removal. Since the optimizer largely combines existing ASAM and GDRO components, the unsupported theoretical and mechanistic claims materially weaken its distinctive contribution. These concerns determine my weak-reject recommendation despite the worthwhile empirical gains.

There are secondary reporting and reproducibility issues. ASGDRO's RxRx1 accuracy is 32.2±0.2% in Table 3 but 30.5±0.1% in Figure 7, without an explanation of different settings. Appendix A.6 specifies the H-CMNIST search grid but does not specify its validation construction or model-selection criterion, which matters for interpreting performance after color removal.
